headline: Approved December 4, 2025 minutes and reviewed CDBG grant and affordable housing issues in Beverly.
summary: The Council approved the December 4, 2025 meeting minutes. Darlene Wynne reported on an $850,000 Community Development Block Grant awarded to the City and plans for a housing rehabilitation program with Habitat for Humanity. Housing advocate Don Preston discussed affordable housing income guidelines, local affordable housing providers, and challenges facing the Beverly Housing Authority, and the Council agreed to discuss these topics further at future meetings.

2. Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) 27 
 28 
Wynne explained that the City was awarded a Community Development Block Grant of 29 
$850,000 for the FY25 round. This was awarded in late October, and the City is working to get it 30 
off the ground. There are three markets for the grant: Entitlement Communities automatically 31 
receive CDBG money and have their own reporting and project implementation plans; Mini 32 
Entitlement Communities have to qualify on a needs basis; finally, the CDBG Community 33 
Development Fund, which is what Beverly applied under. Beverly qualified due to population 34 
size, poverty limit, and the percentage of its population that is low and moderate income. This 35 
award reflects a greater economic divide in the community in terms of a wealth gap. The City 36 
worked with a consultant to prepare the application. The next step is for a housing rehabilitation 37 
program. The City’s intention is to contract with Habitat for Humanity on this project. In 38 
September, the City also learned that it is being reclassified as a Mini Entitlement Community 39 
for the first time in two decades. Thus, for the following three fiscal years this grant is more of a 40 
guarantee. The City will still have to apply each year but does not have to demonstrate the same 41 
need. There was a public hearing last week for the community development strategy, a 3-5 year 42 
plan that list the project goals. She also posted a job on Friday for a part-time fully grant-funded 43 
Grant Manager to help make sure that the program is running appropriately. The goal is to 44

4. Housing Part I – Don Preston, Housing Advocate 52 
 53 
Preston explained that there has been discussion regarding affordable and workforce housing 54 
being an issue for businesses in the area. It is important to understand the HUD guidelines in 55 
terms of area median income to set affordability. Beverly’s local median household income is 56 
approximately $110,000. The regional HUD figure is $31,000 for 30% of area median income 57 
(AMI), $52,000 for 50% AMI, and $83,000 at 80% AMI. The inclusionary zoning is set at 60%/. 58 
Based on Beverley's average income, $83,000 is considered low income. However, even the 59 
most affordable housing programs do not use Beverly’s figure, they use the HUD figure which is 60 
set at approximately $161,000. Even though the City can state that it is creating affordable 61 
housing, it is not truly based on the actual numbers. HUD’s thresholds are much higher than 62 
those derived from Beverly's local information. For example, under the HUD system, a four 63 
person household earning $82,000 is considered very low income or 50%. A household earning 64 
up to $132,000 is considered low income by HUD at 80%. Notably, the HUD 50% level is 65 
roughly equivalent to 80% of Beverly's local income. Wynne explained that it is the geography 66 
encompassed in the HUD figure which sets it to be higher overall.  67 
 68 
Preston explained that a household can earn close to, or even above, Beverly's median income 69 
and still qualify as low income on the HUD standards. This is useful for understanding 70 
affordability within Beverly and for local planning and policy discussions. HUD AMI figures are 71 
the controlling standard for eligibility in most state and federal housing programs, including 72 
Section 8 affordable housing lotteries. Beverly is facing, like most communities, a significant 73 
housing crisis that affects a wide range of residents and local stakeholders. Businesses and 74 
colleges are constantly confronted with the challenge of housing teachers and students. 75 
Businesses also struggle with hiring and retaining workers in this region due to housing costs. 76 
Part of the economic picture is that the City’s workers can't afford to live here. As a result, it is a 77 
struggle to recruit new workers who can afford to live in the area. Meanwhile, elders face 78 
obstacles of downsizing and young families are unable to access affordable housing programs 79 
and options. There is a notable $37,000 difference between HUD and Beverly’s AMI. To more 80 
accurately reflect local income realities, the City could reassess its method for calculating 81 
affordability and update its guidelines accordingly. The City could consider waiving certain fees 82 
for units that are designated as affordable and deed restricted in some way. Real estate taxes 83 
could be modified based on the affordability level of housing units. 84 
 85 
Preston stated that Beverly is served by three main affordable housing developers: Harborlight, 86 
with 192 units; North Shore Community, with 101 units; and the Beverly Housing Authority, 87 
with 646 units. Together, these organizations offer 939 affordable units. The YMCA also 88 
manages some affordable units and there are other organizations that have affordable units in the 89

Preston explained that, if Harborlight cannot take on more people in the 30% AMI range, no one 93 
can.  The Beverly Housing Authority has not developed any new housing since 1950/60. Many 94 
units are single story and require ongoing maintenance and upgrades. A public conversation 95 
should be initiated to explore opportunities for expanding, rebuilding, and upgrading existing 96 
units using state, federal, and private funding sources. Similar initiatives have been done in 97 
nearby communities, such as Gloucester. As the Housing Authority has control over the land, 98 
most of these locations could be doubled in size by adding another floor. The majority of their 99 
units, approximately 558, are for elders. Thus, there is very little affordable housing at this level 100 
for working families and the waitlists are beyond belief. 101 
 102 
Preston stated that the Beverly Housing Authority sits apart as an independent organization, but 103 
it is part of the community and there is a lot of potential in their properties which does not exist 104 
anywhere else in the City. These are underused properties which could help the economic 105 
development of the City. This will require major conversations. The Housing Authority is faced 106 
with limited resources. They are underfunded by the State and underfunded by the federal 107 
government. Even the city of Beverly does not truly support it. These are the blockages. There 108 
may be entities willing to partner with the Housing Authority and develop units. The Housing 109 
Authority also has to be amenable to working with Harborlight. 110
